claims.text: Replacing conventional dipping and plating components with a refractory high-entropy alloy will reduce erosion during hot-dip aluminum plating.
Refractory high-entropy alloys have elevated melting points.
The elevated melting point of an RHEA helps protect it from attack by high-temperature liquid aluminum.
RHEAs tend to form oxide phases.
A bulk RHEA based on Nb, Ta, Ti, and V can be fabricated as a homogeneous solid-solution material.
The proposed RHEA can be supplied in a defect-controlled state.
Hot-dip aluminum plating exposes components to molten aluminum near or slightly above 660°C for long periods.
A stable refractory oxide layer containing Nb or Ta oxides will form on the RHEA during molten-aluminum exposure.
The proposed Nb- or Ta-containing oxide layer will limit further aluminum attack.
Refractory elements in the alloy are chemically inert under the proposed molten-aluminum conditions.
The high melting point and chemical inertness of the refractory elements promote formation of a protective oxide scale.
The oxide scale acts as a barrier that minimizes corrosive interactions between the RHEA substrate and liquid aluminum.
RHEA components will have significantly lower erosion rates than carbon or alloy steel components under identical hot-dip aluminum plating conditions.
The lower erosion rate of RHEA components will extend equipment service life.
Carbon and alloy steel components undergo severe erosion and reduced service life during prolonged exposure to liquid aluminum.
Protective-oxide effectiveness and corrosion resistance depend on alloy composition, processing history, and thermal cycling.
Extreme or fluctuating thermal and mechanical stresses can compromise the proposed protective behavior.
Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit promising mechanical properties and high-temperature phase stability.
Experimental data on RHEA corrosion rates and protective-oxide behavior specifically in molten aluminum are limited.
